Most lung cancer cases are caused by [tobacco smoking](/wiki/Tobacco_smoking "Tobacco smoking"). The remainder are caused by exposure to hazardous substances like [asbestos](/wiki/Asbestos "Asbestos") and [radon](/wiki/Radon "Radon") gas, or by [genetic mutations](/wiki/Genetic_mutation "Genetic mutation") that arise by chance. Consequently, lung cancer prevention efforts encourage people to avoid hazardous chemicals and quit smoking. Quitting smoking both reduces one's chance of developing lung cancer and improves treatment outcomes in those already diagnosed with lung cancer.

Lung cancer is the most diagnosed and deadliest cancer worldwide, with 2.2 million cases in 2020 resulting in 1.8 million deaths.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESungFerlaySiegelLaversanne2021"Lung_cancer"-4) Lung cancer is rare in those younger than 40; the average age at diagnosis is 70 years, and the average age at death 72.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBadeDela_Cruz2020"Age"-3) Incidence and outcomes vary widely across the world, depending on patterns of tobacco use. Prior to the advent of cigarette smoking in the 20th century, lung cancer was a rare disease. In the 1950s and 1960s, increasing evidence linked lung cancer and tobacco use, culminating in declarations by most large national health bodies discouraging tobacco use.

*Star Wars: The Force Awakens* grossed $936.7 million in the United States and Canada and $1.132 billion in other countries for a worldwide total of $2.07 billion,[[3]](#cite_note-BOM-3) making it the [highest-grossing film of 2015](/wiki/2015_in_film#Highest-grossing_films "2015 in film")[[293]](#cite_note-Top2015Films-297) and the [third highest-grossing film of all time](/wiki/List_of_highest-grossing_films "List of highest-grossing films").[[294]](#cite_note-298) [Box Office Mojo](/wiki/Box_Office_Mojo "Box Office Mojo") estimates that the film sold close to 110 million tickets in the United States and Canada.[[295]](#cite_note-299) *The Force Awakens* earned 8.6% of the total 2015 releases in the United States and Canada, second only to the 8.8% of the box office earned by *[Titanic](/wiki/Titanic_(1997_film) "Titanic (1997 film)")* in 1997.[[296]](#cite_note-300) It was the 24th film in cinematic history to gross $1 billion worldwide, standing as the [fastest film](/wiki/List_of_fastest-grossing_films "List of fastest-grossing films") to surpass the mark at the time, doing so in 12 days.[[297]](#cite_note-fastest-to-1b-301) It was also the third film in history to surpass $2 billion worldwide, doing so on its 53rd day of release.[[298]](#cite_note-302) *Deadline Hollywood* calculated the film's net profit as $780.1 million, accounting for production budgets,[[e]](#cite_note-303) marketing, talent participations, and other costs; box office grosses and home media revenues placed it first on their list of 2015's "Most Valuable Blockbusters".[[173]](#cite_note-DeadlineProfitAnalysisFinal-177)

Aspect's experiments, following the first experiment of [Stuart Freedman](/wiki/Stuart_Freedman "Stuart Freedman") and [John Clauser](/wiki/John_Clauser "John Clauser") in 1972, were considered to provide further support to the thesis that [Bell's inequalities](/wiki/Bell%27s_theorem "Bell's theorem") are violated in its [CHSH](/wiki/CHSH_Bell_test "CHSH Bell test") version, in particular by closing a form of the [locality loophole](/wiki/Bell_test_loopholes "Bell test loopholes"). However, his results were not completely conclusive since there were loopholes that allowed for alternative explanations that comply with [local realism](/wiki/Principle_of_locality "Principle of locality").[[13]](#cite_note-13)

After his work on Bell's inequalities, Aspect turned toward studies of [laser cooling](/wiki/Laser_cooling "Laser cooling") of neutral atoms, and [Bose–Einstein condensates](/wiki/Bose%E2%80%93Einstein_condensate "Bose–Einstein condensate") at the [Kastler-Brossel Laboratory](/wiki/Kastler-Brossel_Laboratory "Kastler-Brossel Laboratory").[[14]](#cite_note-14)
